title: Beginner Pack 10
subtitle: Means of Travel, Exemplary Lists & Conversational Nuance
label: 3 patterns · 6 questions
description: Express means and transport with で (paired with destination に), cite representative examples with non-exhaustive や, and navigate conversational intent with sentence-ending particles よ (informing) and ね (seeking agreement).
sources: Komorebi original conversational exchanges for everyday beginner Japanese
JLPT N5 Particles Reference: で means (112#3), や listing (469#1), よ certainty (471#1), ね confirmation (472#1)

patterns.readingNote: で marks the method or vehicle used to travel (e.g. バスで行く = go by bus). Destination continues to use reviewed particle に (駅に行きます), never confusing means with destination.
patterns.summary: In Pack 5, you learned で for the place where an action occurs (店で買います). Here, で marks the means, vehicle, or instrument used to accomplish an action (電車で行きます = go by train). Destinations continue using reviewed に (駅に行きます). We avoid introducing the deferred particle へ here, maintaining clear consistency with destination に.

examples.reading: バスで えきに いきます。
examples.gloss: バスで by bus · 駅に to the station · 行きます go
examples.english: I go to the station by bus.

examples.japanese: 電車でホテルに行きます。
examples.reading: でんしゃで ホテルに いきます。
examples.gloss: 電車で by train · ホテルに to the hotel · 行きます go
examples.english: I go to the hotel by train.

questions.prompt: What does this conversational exchange mean?
questions.japanese: A: 駅まで何で行きますか。 B: バスで行きます。
questions.reading: A: えきまで なんで いきますか。 B: バスで いきます。
questions.gloss: 駅まで to the station · 何で by what / how · 行きますか do you go? · バスで by bus · 行きます go.

choices.text: “Are you walking to the station?” “I am taking the bus.”
choices.explanation: Not quite. 何で asks "by what means / how", not whether the speaker is walking.

choices.text: “How do you go to the station?” “I go by bus.”
choices.explanation: That’s right! 何で asks for the means of transport, and バスで answers that the person travels by bus.

choices.text: “Where does the bus go?” “It goes to the station.”
choices.explanation: Not quite. The first speaker asks how to get to the station (何で行きますか), not where the bus is traveling.

followUp.prompt: What does this conversational exchange mean?
followUp.japanese: A: ホテルまで何で行きますか。 B: 電車で行きます。
followUp.reading: A: ホテルまで なんで いきますか。 B: でんしゃで いきます。
followUp.gloss: ホテルまで to the hotel · 何で by what / how · 行きますか do you go? · 電車で by train · 行きます go.

choices.text: “When do you go to the hotel?” “I go by train.”
choices.explanation: Not quite. 何で asks "by what means / how", not "when" (いつ).

choices.text: “Who is going to the hotel?” “The train is going.”
choices.explanation: Not quite. 何で asks about means of travel, not who is going (だれ).

choices.text: “How do you go to the hotel?” “I go by train.”
choices.explanation: That’s right! 何で asks for the means of transport, and 電車で specifies going by train.

workedExample.japanese: 「学校まで何で行きますか。」「自転車で行きます。」
workedExample.english: “How do you go to school?” “I go by bicycle.”
workedExample.breakdown: 何で (nande) asks for the means or method of transportation. 自転車で (jitensha de) marks the vehicle with で to express "by bicycle".

dialogue.japanese: ホテルまで何で行きますか。
dialogue.reading: ホテルまで なんで いきますか。

dialogue.speaker: B

dialogue.speaker: A

questions.prompt: Which particle correctly marks the means of transport to the station?
questions.japanese: 私は駅に電車（　）行きます。
questions.reading: わたしは えきに でんしゃ（　）いきます。
questions.gloss: 私は I · 駅に to the station · 電車 by train · 行きます go

choices.explanation: That’s right! で marks the vehicle or means of travel (電車で = by train), while に marks the destination (駅に).
Not quite. に marks the target or destination (already present in 駅に); for the vehicle or means of transport, use で.
Not quite. を marks a direct grammatical object (like 水を飲みます); transportation methods take で.

followUp.prompt: Which particle correctly marks the vehicle used to travel to the hotel?
followUp.japanese: 友だちはホテルに車（　）行きます。
followUp.reading: ともだちは ホテルに くるま（　）いきます。
followUp.gloss: 友だちは my friend · ホテルに to the hotel · 車 by car · 行きます goes

choices.explanation: Not quite. に marks destinations or points in time; 車 is the vehicle used, which requires で.
That’s right! で indicates the means or vehicle used for travel (車で = by car), while に marks the destination (ホテルに).
Not quite. を indicates the direct object of a transitive action; traveling by a vehicle takes で.

workedExample.japanese: 田中さんは山にバスで行きます。
workedExample.english: Tanaka-san goes to the mountain by bus.
workedExample.breakdown: 山に (yama ni) specifies the destination with に, and バスで (basu de) marks the vehicle with で.

patterns.gloss: A and B (among other things / representative examples)
patterns.readingNote: や connects nouns to cite examples from a larger or non-exhaustive group (e.g. 本やペン = books, pens, and the like).
patterns.summary: In Pack 3, you learned particle と to connect nouns (山と川 = mountain and river). と presents the nouns together as a specific, defined group. In contrast, や introduces non-exhaustive, representative examples from a larger set (本やペン = things like books and pens). It leaves open that other unmentioned items also exist in the scene.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本やペンがあります。
examples.reading: つくえの うえに ほんや ペンが あります。
examples.gloss: 机の上に on the desk · 本や books, pens, etc. · ペン pen · が subject · あります there are
examples.english: There are things like books and pens on the desk.

examples.japanese: 部屋に水や果物があります。
examples.reading: へやに みずや くだものが あります。
examples.gloss: 部屋に in the room · 水や water, fruit, etc. · 果物 fruit · が subject · あります there are
examples.english: There are things like water and fruit in the room.

questions.prompt: What does this sentence express about the items on the desk?
questions.japanese: 机の上に本やペンがあります。
questions.reading: つくえの うえに ほんや ペンが あります。
questions.gloss: 机の上に on top of the desk · 本や books, pens, etc. · ペン pen · が subject · あります there are

choices.text: There are only two items on the desk: exactly one book and one pen.
choices.explanation: Not quite. Particle や gives examples among others; it does not limit the contents to only those two items.

choices.text: There is a book on top of a pen on the desk.
choices.explanation: Not quite. や connects nouns as listed items ("books and pens"), not one resting on top of the other.

choices.text: There are things like books and pens on the desk (giving representative examples).
choices.explanation: That’s right! Particle や lists representative examples from the desk without claiming those are the only items present.

followUp.prompt: What does this sentence convey about the items in the room?
followUp.japanese: 部屋に水や果物があります。
followUp.reading: へやに みずや くだものが あります。
followUp.gloss: 部屋に in the room · 水や water, fruit, etc. · 果物 fruit · が subject · あります there are

choices.text: There are things such as water and fruit in the room (as representative examples).
choices.explanation: That’s right! Particle や highlights representative items present in the room without restricting the scene to only those items.

choices.text: There is water instead of fruit in the room.
choices.explanation: Not quite. や lists items together as examples, not as mutually exclusive alternatives ("instead of").

choices.text: There is absolutely nothing in the room except water and one fruit.
choices.explanation: Not quite. Particle や is non-exhaustive; it mentions water and fruit as examples, leaving room for other items.

workedExample.japanese: かばんの中に財布や鍵があります。
workedExample.english: There are things like a wallet and keys in the bag.
workedExample.breakdown: や (ya) connects 財布 (wallet) and 鍵 (keys) as illustrative items present, implying other items may also be inside.

questions.prompt: Which particle best completes the sentence to list bread and water as representative items bought at the store?
questions.japanese: 店でパン（　）水を買います。
questions.reading: みせで パン（　）みずを かいます。
questions.gloss: 店で at the store · パン bread · 水 water · を object · 買います buy

choices.explanation: Not quite. で marks location of action (店で) or means; it does not connect two nouns in a list.
That’s right! Particle や connects nouns to list representative examples (パンや水 = things like bread and water).
Not quite. に marks destinations, time, or indirect objects; it does not connect two nouns into a list.

followUp.prompt: Which particle best connects books and paper as representative examples inside the box?
followUp.japanese: 箱の中に本（　）紙があります。
followUp.reading: はこの なかに ほん（　）かみが あります。
followUp.gloss: 箱の中に inside the box · 本 books · 紙 paper · が subject · あります there are

choices.explanation: Not quite. で indicates an action site or tool; it cannot join two nouns to cite them as items in a box.
Not quite. に marks the location (箱の中に); connecting the two listed nouns requires particle や.
That’s right! Particle や connects 本 and 紙 as representative examples of items inside the box.

workedExample.japanese: 庭に木や花があります。
workedExample.english: There are things like trees and flowers in the garden.
workedExample.breakdown: や (ya) links 木 (trees) and 花 (flowers) as representative examples of plants in the garden.

patterns.readingNote: よ informs the listener of something they may not know with friendly certainty. ね seeks mutual agreement or confirms shared experience ('isn't it?').
patterns.summary: Sentence-ending particles enrich natural spoken Japanese: (1) よ shares new information, advice, or polite notice with the listener (駅の入り口はあそこですよ = The station entrance is over there, you know). (2) ね invites agreement or confirms a shared observation (ふじ山は本当に大きいですね = Mt. Fuji really is big, isn't it?). To avoid ambiguity, look closely at the conversational context and speaker intent: is the speaker sharing new information, or asking for shared agreement?

examples.japanese: 「駅の入り口はどこですか。」「あそこですよ。」
examples.reading: 「えきの いりぐちは どこですか。」「あそこですよ。」
examples.gloss: 「駅の入り口 station entrance · は topic · どこですか where is it?」「あそこですよ it is over there (informing)」
examples.english: “Where is the station entrance?” “It is right over there (let me tell you).”

examples.japanese: 「ふじ山は本当に大きいですね。」「そうですね。」
examples.reading: 「ふじさんは ほんとうに おおきいですね。」「そうですね。」
examples.gloss: 「ふじ山 Mt. Fuji · は topic · 本当に really · 大きいですね big, isn't it?」「そうですね that's true」
examples.english: “Mt. Fuji is really big, isn't it?” “It really is.”

questions.prompt: In this dialogue, Person A is asking for directions. Person B informs them where the entrance is. Which ending best fits Person B's intent to inform?
questions.japanese: A: 駅の入り口はどこですか。 B: あそこです（　）。
questions.reading: A: えきの いりぐちは どこですか。 B: あそこです（　）。
questions.gloss: 駅の入り口 station entrance · は topic · どこですか where is it? · あそこです it is over there · （　）

choices.explanation: That’s right! Person A asked for information they did not know; Person B uses よ to inform them with helpful certainty.
Not quite. Particle ね seeks mutual agreement on something both already know; here Person B is providing new information to someone who asked.
Not quite. Particle か would turn Person B's answer into a question ("Is it over there?"), rather than answering Person A's question.

followUp.prompt: In this dialogue, Person A asks if the book is interesting. Person B shares their recommendation to inform Person A. Which ending best expresses Person B's intent to inform?
followUp.japanese: A: この本はおもしろいですか。 B: とてもおもしろい（　）。
followUp.reading: A: この ほんは おもしろいですか。 B: とても おもしろい（　）。
followUp.gloss: この本 this book · は topic · おもしろいですか is it interesting? · とても very · おもしろい interesting · （　）

choices.explanation: Not quite. Particle ね seeks mutual agreement on something both already know; here Person B is informing Person A of their experience.
That’s right! Person B uses ですよ to inform Person A of their experience with friendly certainty.
Not quite. ですか would make Person B's answer into a question rather than answering Person A's question.

workedExample.japanese: 「あの店はおいしいですか。」「おいしいですよ。」
workedExample.english: “Is that restaurant good?” “It’s delicious, let me tell you!”
workedExample.breakdown: The second speaker provides their personal recommendation using よ (yo) to inform the curious listener.

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.japanese: この本はおもしろいですか。
dialogue.reading: この ほんは おもしろいですか。

dialogue.speaker: B
dialogue.reading: とても おもしろい（　）。

dialogue.speaker: A
dialogue.japanese: 駅の入り口はどこですか。
dialogue.reading: えきの いりぐちは どこですか。

questions.prompt: Two friends are looking up at Mount Fuji together on a clear day. Speaker A invites shared agreement on its immense size, and Speaker B immediately agrees. Which sentence ending does Speaker A use to invite shared agreement?
questions.japanese: A: ふじ山は本当に大きい（　）。 B: そうですね。
questions.reading: A: ふじさんは ほんとうに おおきい（　）。 B: そうですね。
questions.gloss: ふじ山 Mt. Fuji · は topic · 本当に really · 大きい big · （　） · そうですね that is so, isn't it

choices.explanation: Not quite. Particle よ informs someone of a fact they do not yet know; here both speakers are gazing at Mount Fuji together, so Speaker A invites agreement with ね.
Not quite. ですか turns the statement into an open question; Speaker A is making an observation and inviting their friend to agree.
That’s right! Both speakers are viewing Mount Fuji together; Speaker A uses ですね to invite mutual agreement, and Speaker B responds with そうですね.

followUp.prompt: Two visitors step into a quiet room. Speaker A remarks on the peaceful atmosphere to invite agreement, and Speaker B immediately agrees. Which sentence ending does Speaker A use to invite mutual agreement?
followUp.japanese: A: この部屋は静か（　）。 B: ええ、静かですね。
followUp.reading: A: この へやは しずか（　）。 B: ええ、しずかですね。
followUp.gloss: この部屋 this room · は topic · 静か quiet · （　） · ええ yes · 静かですね it really is quiet

choices.explanation: That’s right! Both speakers are in the quiet room together; Speaker A uses ですね to invite mutual agreement.
Not quite. Particle よ informs someone of a fact they do not yet know; here both speakers are in the quiet room together, so Speaker A invites agreement with ね.
Not quite. ですか turns the statement into an open question; Speaker A is making an observation and inviting their friend to agree.

workedExample.japanese: 「今日はいい天気ですね。」「そうですね。」
workedExample.english: “The weather is nice today, isn't it?” “It sure is.”
workedExample.breakdown: ね (ne) is used when both people are experiencing the same situation (the pleasant weather) to share a friendly moment of agreement.
